directAnswer: Pope Paul IV was Gian Pietro Carafa, co-founder of the Theatine order and a leading figure of the Roman Inquisition, who reigned from 1555 to 1559. A severe reformer, he established the Roman Ghetto with the bull Cum nimis absurdum, published the first papal Index of Forbidden Books, and fought a disastrous war against Spain.

paras: Gian Pietro Carafa was born on 28 June 1476 at Capriglia Irpina near Avellino, in the Kingdom of Naples, into a powerful Neapolitan family. He served as a papal diplomat, including in England and Spain, and became bishop of Chieti, whose Latin name Theate later gave a name to his religious order.

In 1524 he resigned his benefices and joined St. Cajetan of Thiene in founding the Theatines, a community of priests committed to poverty and pastoral reform. Paul III made him a cardinal in 1536, and he served on the 1537 reform commission.

Carafa was a principal promoter of the Roman Inquisition established in 1542 and directed it with great severity. Elected pope on 23 May 1555 at nearly 79, he continued that approach, pursuing even respected cardinals such as Giovanni Morone, whom he imprisoned on suspicion of heresy.

In 1559 he published the first Index of Forbidden Books issued by a pope, so sweeping that it was moderated by his successor. He also pressed Michelangelo's Last Judgment as indecent; the covering of its nudes was carried out only after his death.

sections.h2: Cum Nimis Absurdum and the Roman Ghetto
paras: In July 1555 Paul IV issued the bull Cum nimis absurdum, which confined Rome's Jews to a walled quarter near the Tiber, required them to wear a distinguishing sign, and restricted their trades and property. The Roman Ghetto lasted until 1870.

The Church today regards such measures with deep regret. Recent popes have visited Rome's synagogue, which stands near the site of the old ghetto, as a sign of a very different relationship with the Jewish people.

sections.h2: War with Spain and the Fall of the Carafa Nephews
paras: Fiercely hostile to Spanish rule over Naples, Paul IV allied with France against Philip II. In 1556 and 1557 the Duke of Alba's army invaded the Papal States, and the pope was forced to make peace.

His nephew Cardinal Carlo Carafa had driven much of this policy. In 1559 Paul IV discovered his nephews' misconduct, stripped them of office and banished them from Rome. When he died on 18 August 1559, crowds tore down his statue on the Capitol and attacked the offices of the Inquisition.

keyFacts: Born Gian Pietro Carafa at Capriglia Irpina on 28 June 1476
Co-founded the Theatines with St. Cajetan of Thiene (1524)
Issued Cum nimis absurdum establishing the Roman Ghetto (1555)
Published the first papal Index of Forbidden Books (1559)
Fought a losing war against Spain (1556 to 1557)

faqs.question: What was Cum nimis absurdum?
faqs.answer: A 1555 bull of Paul IV that confined Rome's Jews to a walled ghetto and imposed severe restrictions on them. The ghetto remained until 1870, and the Church now recognizes such measures as grave wrongs.

faqs.question: How are the Theatines connected to Paul IV?
faqs.answer: As Gian Pietro Carafa he co-founded the order with St. Cajetan of Thiene in 1524. The name comes from Theate, the Latin name of Chieti, where Carafa had been bishop.

faqs.question: Did Paul IV have the Last Judgment painted over?
faqs.answer: He objected to its nudity, but the draperies were added by Daniele da Volterra after his death, following a decree of the Council of Trent in 1563.
